title: Using a proforma to improve standards of documentation of an orthopaedic post-take ward round.
standard: GMC and Royal College of Physicians documentation recommendations: clearly documented PTWR, date/time, consultant on take, clinician leading and documenting, presenting complaint and management plan
finding: 72% seen on PTWR, 47% of these clearly labelled; 64% of those not seen were weekend admissions; no consultant on take identifiable in 19%, presenting complaint missing in 78%, no plan in 3%, not timed in 17%, no name 19%, no signature 14%, no grade 50%, no contact details 25%.
change: Trauma Meeting/Post-Take Ward Round proforma on yellow paper, designed with the team (PDSA cycles), results presented at departmental teaching, and weekend surgical juniors briefed to attend the trauma meeting and complete it.
setting: District general hospital trauma and orthopaedic department (population 320,000, consultant-led 24/7 trauma service)
cycle1_result: 72% seen on PTWR, 47% of these clearly labelled; 64% of those not seen were weekend admissions; no consultant on take identifiable in 19%, presenting complaint missing in 78%, no plan in 3%, not timed in 17%, no name 19%, no signature 14%, no grade 50%, no contact details 25%.
intervention: Trauma Meeting/Post-Take Ward Round proforma on yellow paper, designed with the team (PDSA cycles), results presented at departmental teaching, and weekend surgical juniors briefed to attend the trauma meeting and complete it.
cycle2_period: Prospective re-audit two weeks after implementation
cycle2_result: Not seen on PTWR fell from 28% to 18% (4% weekend admissions); 88% of those seen had a proforma; 18% of all cases had no proforma; consultant unidentifiable in 4%; all entries signed and dated; no name 12%, no contact details 15%, no grade 10%.
other_findings: Weekend proforma completion stayed poor (67% of cases without a proforma were weekend admissions); all remaining documentation gaps were in cases without a proforma.

title: Medical rota changes and venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in orthopaedic patients.

finding: 71% of patients compliant with all measures; errors mainly medical (failure to prescribe LMWH or stockings, incorrect dosing), plus nursing and patient errors; about 30% of surveyed patients (n=47) understood aims of VTE prophylaxis.
change: Policy of prophylaxis unless contraindicated, summarised guidelines displayed on wards, MDT teaching for doctors and nurses, patient education, VTE added to handover and radiology meeting, teaching after rota change, and VTE education added to junior doctor induction.
setting: Trauma and orthopaedic unit, Monklands District General Hospital, NHS Lanarkshire (emergency admissions)
cycle1_result: 71% of patients compliant with all measures; errors mainly medical (failure to prescribe LMWH or stockings, incorrect dosing), plus nursing and patient errors; about 30% of surveyed patients (n=47) understood aims of VTE prophylaxis.
intervention: Policy of prophylaxis unless contraindicated, summarised guidelines displayed on wards, MDT teaching for doctors and nurses, patient education, VTE added to handover and radiology meeting, teaching after rota change, and VTE education added to junior doctor induction.
cycle2_result: Re-audit 4: 100% compliance; 80% of patients understood aims of VTE prophylaxis.

title: Continuity of care for orthopaedic patients in a district general hospital.
standard: Local standard from patient survey: a patient should be seen by the same surgeon from preoperative clinic to surgery and postoperative follow-up
finding: Same surgeon throughout 23%; same team 43%; operated on by clinic surgeon 50%; followed up by operating surgeon 40%; trauma continuity 10%.
change: Trauma on-call rota reorganised to weekly consultant 'on take' so the admitting team operates, and ward clerk booked follow-up into the operating surgeon's clinic.
setting: Orthopaedic department, James Paget University Hospital (district general hospital), elective and trauma lists
cycle1_result: Same surgeon throughout 23%; same team 43%; operated on by clinic surgeon 50%; followed up by operating surgeon 40%; trauma continuity 10%.
intervention: Trauma on-call rota reorganised to weekly consultant 'on take' so the admitting team operates, and ward clerk booked follow-up into the operating surgeon's clinic.
cycle2_result: Same surgeon throughout 24%; same team 56%; operated on by clinic surgeon 60%; followed up by operating surgeon 43%; trauma same team 75%.

cycle1_result: BPT achieved in 8/18 (44.4%); 4 waited >36 h for surgery, 7 >72 h for orthogeriatric review, 9 lacked both AMT scores; FI block in ED 3/18 (16.7%)

title: Improving the availability of intra-operative images created during trauma operations - a multidisciplinary team collaboration.

cycle1_result: 9/27 (33%) images available within 72 hours; 4 (15%) delayed by failure to request, 14 (52%) requested but not processed

finding: Poor handover: patient location 57%, responsible consultant 14%, results of significant/pending investigations 29%, co-morbidities 38%, outstanding tasks 38%; one patient not handed over and one nerve injury not handed over.
change: Trauma-specific paper handover proforma (SHOs informed by email and verbally), then an electronic proforma accessible from any hospital computer, created with IT.

cycle1_result: Poor handover: patient location 57%, responsible consultant 14%, results of significant/pending investigations 29%, co-morbidities 38%, outstanding tasks 38%; one patient not handed over and one nerve injury not handed over.
intervention: Trauma-specific paper handover proforma (SHOs informed by email and verbally), then an electronic proforma accessible from any hospital computer, created with IT.

cycle1_result: Of 204 patients coded as subtrochanteric fractures, 178 had radiographic evidence of other fracture types. Of 193 with radiographs reviewed, 24 (12.4%) met AFF criteria; radiologists had diagnosed AFF in only 1 of the 24.

cycle1_result: Positive sites: nose 69.60% (n=96), groin 26.10% (n=36), throat 25.30% (n=35), axilla 8.70% (n=12); a nose, groin and throat three-swab policy would miss 2.2%.

finding: 162/184 (88.0%) referred for VFC review; 98.1% reached afterwards (3 patients, 1.9%, not reached); 29/162 (17.9%) discharged 'virtually'; 137/291 (45.0%) appointments remote. Median total ED time 95 minutes vs 131 minutes at baseline (p<0.001).

cycle1_result: 162/184 (88.0%) referred for VFC review; 98.1% reached afterwards (3 patients, 1.9%, not reached); 29/162 (17.9%) discharged 'virtually'; 137/291 (45.0%) appointments remote. Median total ED time 95 minutes vs 131 minutes at baseline (p<0.001).

finding: Handwritten summaries: complications in hospital 50%, contact information 34%, condition at discharge 66%, understandability 58%, allergies 66%, problem list/issues pending 35%, discharge medications 88%, follow-up plan 80%; patient signature 0%
change: Introduction of electronic discharge summaries using a standardised form completed by orthopaedic residents (from 8 January 2022)
setting: Orthopaedics department, MVJ Medical College and Research Hospital, tertiary care hospital, Bangalore
cycle1_period: Audited between May 22 and October 22 (handwritten summaries, before electronic summaries introduced on 8 January 2022)
cycle1_result: Handwritten summaries: complications in hospital 50%, contact information 34%, condition at discharge 66%, understandability 58%, allergies 66%, problem list/issues pending 35%, discharge medications 88%, follow-up plan 80%; patient signature 0%
intervention: Introduction of electronic discharge summaries using a standardised form completed by orthopaedic residents (from 8 January 2022)

topic: Paediatric buckle and forearm fracture management
title: Early Management of Paediatric Wrist and Forearm Fractures in a Busy District General Hospital Emergency Department: A Retrospective Cohort Comparison Study and Audit of BOAST Guidelines.
standard: BOAST early management of distal forearm fractures in children (May 2021): early ED manipulation, neurovascular and consent documentation, orthogonal X-rays, fracture clinic within 7 days
finding: 23/72 (31.94%) manipulated in ED; 11 of 23 ED manipulations failed.
change: Local trust pathway in line with BOAST introduced from July 2021 (analgesia/sedation, location, manipulation and referral guidance) with staff education.
setting: Emergency department, district general hospital with paediatric orthopaedic services, Gloucestershire Royal Hospital
cycle1_result: 23/72 (31.94%) manipulated in ED; 11 of 23 ED manipulations failed.
intervention: Local trust pathway in line with BOAST introduced from July 2021 (analgesia/sedation, location, manipulation and referral guidance) with staff education.
cycle2_result: 73/87 manipulated in ED (p<0.00001); 63 (86.31%) acceptable reduction, 10 (13.69%) failed. BOAST compliance: neurovascular documentation pre-manipulation 93.10% (81/87), before discharge 64.36% (56/87); consent documentation 73.56% (64/87); orthogonal X-rays 100% (87/87); fracture clinic within 7 days 49.42% (43/87), mean 8.25 days.
other_findings: Reasons for not attempting ED manipulation (14 cases) were not documented; about 63 hours of theatre time saved. Protocol changed so off-ended fractures are manipulated under sedation.

title: Orthopaedic Out of Bed Project (OOBP): improving early mobilisation following femoral fracture using a therapy-led education programme.
standard: NHFD metric: patient mobilised (standing or hoisted) out of bed by the day after surgery; target at least the UK national average of 81%
finding: Mean 60% of patients mobilised by the day after surgery. Hip Sprint cohort (n=60): 1.7% mobilised by healthcare assistants before physiotherapy assessment.
change: Therapy-led ward education programme for trauma healthcare assistants (1-hour 2:1 face-to-face session plus observed sign-off), ward posters and Trust media campaign, delivered over two PDSA cycles (June-July 2020 and June-August 2022)
setting: 35-bed trauma ward, James Paget University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust (district general hospital), Great Yarmouth
cycle1_period: 6 months before the intervention (2019/2020, NHFD data); Hip Sprint audit September and December 2019
cycle1_result: Mean 60% of patients mobilised by the day after surgery. Hip Sprint cohort (n=60): 1.7% mobilised by healthcare assistants before physiotherapy assessment.
intervention: Therapy-led ward education programme for trauma healthcare assistants (1-hour 2:1 face-to-face session plus observed sign-off), ward posters and Trust media campaign, delivered over two PDSA cycles (June-July 2020 and June-August 2022)
cycle2_result: Mean 79.2% mobilised by the day after surgery after PDSA cycle 2 (from 60% in 2019). Healthcare assistant mobilisation before physiotherapy assessment 30% (n=51 cohort).
other_findings: After PDSA cycle 1 the rate rose to a mean of 78% but fell back to 71.8% in 2021, attributed to staff turnover. 30-day mortality fell from 10.1% to 7% between 2019 and 2022 (causality not established).

title: An Audit on the Pre-operative Fasting Time of Trauma-List Orthopaedic Patients at a District General Hospital in Chichester, United Kingdom.
standard: RCN, AAGBI, European Society of Anaesthesiology and ASA guidelines: fasting of two hours for clear fluids and six hours for solids
finding: All 50 patients (100%) fasted beyond six hours for solids (mean 15.8 hours, range 9–24) and 49 (98%) beyond two hours for clear fluids (mean 10.5 hours, range 2–20); only 5 (10%) had correct documented fasting instructions; 31 (62%) were 'nil by mouth from midnight'.
setting: Orthopaedic trauma list, St Richard's Hospital, district general hospital, Chichester
cycle1_result: All 50 patients (100%) fasted beyond six hours for solids (mean 15.8 hours, range 9–24) and 49 (98%) beyond two hours for clear fluids (mean 10.5 hours, range 2–20); only 5 (10%) had correct documented fasting instructions; 31 (62%) were 'nil by mouth from midnight'.
other_findings: Staff survey showed poor knowledge: only 42.9% of ward nurses knew the 6 hour/2 hour rule. Only 52% received preoperative IV fluids; a 'sip till send' policy has since been introduced.
authors: Perera H; Wusu A; Mohammad A; Qulaghassi MZ; Abdulkarim A

finding: Infection documented in 98.4%, blood clots 95.2%, bleeding 92.1%, neurovascular injury 79.4%, dislocation 77.8%, pain 74.6%, anaesthetic complications 73%, failure 68.3%, leg length discrepancy 60.3%, bone damage/fracture 50.8%, death 49.2%, wound complications 42.9%, hip stiffness 14.3%, catheterisation 0%. setting: St Richard's Hospital, Chichester; district general hospital trauma and orthopaedic department
cycle1_result: Infection documented in 98.4%, blood clots 95.2%, bleeding 92.1%, neurovascular injury 79.4%, dislocation 77.8%, pain 74.6%, anaesthetic complications 73%, failure 68.3%, leg length discrepancy 60.3%, bone damage/fracture 50.8%, death 49.2%, wound complications 42.9%, hip stiffness 14.3%, catheterisation 0%. title: Development of a New Knee Arthroscopy Operative Proforma Saving Thousands of British Pounds.
standard: Correct ICD-10 and OPCS-4 coding of arthroscopic knee procedures from the operation note; proforma based on Royal College guidance for operation notes
finding: 17/34 (50%) cases coded incorrectly; tariff value £85,026 as coded versus £114,351 after correction, a loss of £29,325.
change: New coding-friendly knee arthroscopy operation note proforma with tick boxes, developed with coding staff and agreed at a consensus meeting, disseminated by email, notice boards and governance meetings.
setting: Two centres of one trauma and orthopaedic service (Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust / North Manchester General Hospital), knee arthroscopy day cases
cycle1_result: 17/34 (50%) cases coded incorrectly; tariff value £85,026 as coded versus £114,351 after correction, a loss of £29,325.
intervention: New coding-friendly knee arthroscopy operation note proforma with tick boxes, developed with coding staff and agreed at a consensus meeting, disseminated by email, notice boards and governance meetings.
cycle2_result: 2/37 (5%) cases coded incorrectly; £86,886 as coded versus £89,540 after correction, a loss of £2654.
other_findings: Most coding errors came from vague documentation of preoperative diagnoses and additional procedures (e.g. extra meniscectomy or cartilage debridement). Uptake of the proforma was slow and some cases were excluded for incorrect use of the form.

finding: Mechanism of injury 86%; skin integrity 54%; circulation status 54%; detailed vascular examination 17%; neurological examination 54%; sensory detail 48%; MRC motor scale 48%; repeat neurovascular examination after reduction 56%; overall precise documentation of clinical findings 17%.
change: Targeted education on documentation standards at induction and trauma meetings, with case-based discussion reports; made a permanent part of departmental teaching.

cycle1_result: Mechanism of injury 86%; skin integrity 54%; circulation status 54%; detailed vascular examination 17%; neurological examination 54%; sensory detail 48%; MRC motor scale 48%; repeat neurovascular examination after reduction 56%; overall precise documentation of clinical findings 17%.

topic: Suspected cauda equina time to MRI

standard: NICE, BASS and SBNS guidelines and local trust protocol; National Suspected CES Pathway recommends MRI within four hours of request
finding: Mean MRI waiting time 12.5 hours (8am-4pm 9.5 h; 4pm-12am 18 h; 12am-8am 8.5 h); same-day discharge 27 (29%); inpatient stay 66 (71%)
change: Introduction of a middle-grade trauma and orthopaedic doctor in the emergency department (urgent treatment centre) to assess suspected CES patients
setting: Wythenshawe Hospital, Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, a district general hospital with no on-site spinal services; trauma and orthopaedic referrals from the emergency department
cycle1_result: Mean MRI waiting time 12.5 hours (8am-4pm 9.5 h; 4pm-12am 18 h; 12am-8am 8.5 h); same-day discharge 27 (29%); inpatient stay 66 (71%)
intervention: Introduction of a middle-grade trauma and orthopaedic doctor in the emergency department (urgent treatment centre) to assess suspected CES patients

title: Improving Completion Rates of Treatment Escalation Plan (TEP) in a London Teaching Hospital: A Quality Improvement Study.
standard: Trust treatment escalation plan (TEP) policy: TEP completed for emergency adult admissions, within 48 hours
finding: Overall TEP completion 69.5%; completed within 48 hours 47.82%; mean time to complete 4.4 days; mean overrides 3.2; longest 35 days; 24 instances of skipping. Incomplete TEPs 30.4% (n=7).
change: Revised local TEP pathway/algorithm allowing F1+ doctors to complete TEPs for young patients with simple fractures, algorithm displayed in trauma room, emails, individual teaching, and reminders to discuss TEP status on the post-take ward round.
setting: Orthopaedic wards, University Hospital Lewisham (London teaching hospital), adult inpatients
cycle1_result: Overall TEP completion 69.5%; completed within 48 hours 47.82%; mean time to complete 4.4 days; mean overrides 3.2; longest 35 days; 24 instances of skipping. Incomplete TEPs 30.4% (n=7).
intervention: Revised local TEP pathway/algorithm allowing F1+ doctors to complete TEPs for young patients with simple fractures, algorithm displayed in trauma room, emails, individual teaching, and reminders to discuss TEP status on the post-take ward round.
cycle2_result: Overall completion 88.2%; completed within 48 hours 35.29%; mean time 3.7 days; mean overrides 1.3; longest 13 days; 5 instances of skipping. Incomplete TEPs 11.76% (n=2).

topic: Elective cancellations due to asymptomatic bacteriuria
title: Introduction of a New Protocol to Limit the Number of Cancelled Elective Orthopaedic Operations Due to Asymptomatic Bacteriuria.
standard: not reported
finding: Of 33 all-cause cancellations, 7 (21.2%) were cancelled for UTI risk on positive urinalysis; only 1 (14.3%) of these was symptomatic, so 6 (85.7%) were cancelled for asymptomatic bacteriuria.
change: New symptom-based protocol from 1 May 2019: all patients complete a 7-item UTI symptom questionnaire and surgery is cancelled only if two or more symptoms are reported, regardless of urinalysis.
setting: Lister Hospital, Stevenage (East & North Herts NHS Trust), large district general hospital offering tertiary orthopaedic services; cancelled elective orthopaedic operations
cycle1_result: Of 33 all-cause cancellations, 7 (21.2%) were cancelled for UTI risk on positive urinalysis; only 1 (14.3%) of these was symptomatic, so 6 (85.7%) were cancelled for asymptomatic bacteriuria.
intervention: New symptom-based protocol from 1 May 2019: all patients complete a 7-item UTI symptom questionnaire and surgery is cancelled only if two or more symptoms are reported, regardless of urinalysis.
cycle2_result: Of 45 all-cause cancellations, 2 (4.4%) were cancelled for UTI risk, both symptomatic; 4 (8.8%) had positive urinalysis, the 2 asymptomatic ones cancelled for unrelated reasons. No cancellations for asymptomatic bacteriuria; estimated 71.4% reduction in cancellations for UTI risk.
other_findings: Patients with positive urinalysis whose operations were not cancelled were not captured, so the true effect is estimated. Each cancelled operation was estimated to waste 2.1 hours of theatre time (about £2,525).
authors: Taylor N; Jaques A; Antar M; Raghu A; Tai S
citation: Taylor N, Jaques A, Antar M, Raghu A, Tai S. Introduction of a New Protocol to Limit the Number of Cancelled Elective Orthopaedic Operations Due to Asymptomatic Bacteriuria. Cureus. 2023;15(12):e51097. doi:10.7759/cureus.51097. PMID: 38274927.

topic: Paediatric buckle and forearm fracture management
title: Clinical Audit of Manipulation of Paediatric Forearm Fractures in the Emergency Department at a District General Hospital: A Quality Improvement Project.

finding: Pre-implementation (n=11 suitable fractures): manipulation in ED 1 (9.1%); theatre required 4 (36.4%).

cycle1_result: Pre-implementation (n=11 suitable fractures): manipulation in ED 1 (9.1%); theatre required 4 (36.4%).
intervention: New standard operating procedure and paediatric fracture manipulation pathway in the ED using intranasal fentanyl and Entonox, agreed with ED, orthopaedics, radiology and theatre managers; information leaflets planned after cycle 2.
cycle2_result: Third cycle (n=52): manipulation in ED 9 (17.3%); theatre required 1 (1.9%). All nine manipulable fractures were manipulated in the ED.

title: Improving the Safety of Tourniquet Use in a Trauma Theatre According to the British Orthopaedic Association Guidelines: A Closed Loop Audit.
standard: BOAST guidance on the safe use of intraoperative tourniquets (2021): document skin condition and isolation method, pressure SBP + 50-100 mmHg upper limb and + 70-130 mmHg lower limb in adults, ischaemic time under 120 minutes

change: Three PDSA cycles (July 2023 to January 2024): CES working group and trust-level awareness; new locally adapted SOP based on the GIRFT pathway with CES-specific shorter MRI sequences; ED triage and assessment posters, board round, grand round and senior-led teaching. Planned extension of MRI hours was not achieved.

cycle1_result: Median time from ED presentation to MRI 5.9 hours (IQR 4.9–14.7) although median MRI request to scan was 1.7 hours (IQR 1.1–3.7), meeting the GIRFT target; 8% of patients incorrectly sent to the GP-led MEDOCC service. intervention: Three PDSA cycles (July 2023 to January 2024): CES working group and trust-level awareness; new locally adapted SOP based on the GIRFT pathway with CES-specific shorter MRI sequences; ED triage and assessment posters, board round, grand round and senior-led teaching. cycle1_result: MRI utilisation 77.7% (269/346). standard: National waste management guidance: infectious (orange) stream only for suspected infectious agents, otherwise offensive (tiger-stripe) and general streams; no numerical target stated

setting: Ten UK NHS trusts, elective primary total hip and knee arthroplasty (prospective multicentre audit)
cycle1_result: 92 THAs and 130 TKAs; mean total waste 14.79 kg per THA and 13.61 kg per TKA; infectious waste the largest category (9.88 kg THA, 8.68 kg TKA). standard: AUGIS guidelines: laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 72 hours for biliary colic and cholecystitis, within 2 weeks for gallstone pancreatitis

cycle1_result: Biliary colic (9 pre-COVID, 5 during COVID): none had LC within 72 hours. Cholecystitis (20 pre-COVID, 16 during COVID): none within 72 hours; 5 per group had LC, with longer waits during COVID. Gallstone pancreatitis: only 1 had LC within 2 weeks

authors: Mewse J; Ledda V; Connor E; Mason P

title: OGC P09 Benchmarking of OG cancer care across the United Kingdom: a collaboration of 2 national clinical audit systems
standard: not reported
finding: Staging CT: England 83.1%, Scotland 98.5%, Wales 92.2%. MDT curative treatment plans: England 40%, Scotland 29%, Wales 34%; actual curative treatment 24–31%. Longitudinal margin positivity: Scotland 2.4%, England 5.4%, Wales 8.2%.

title: OGC P35 A clinical audit looking at how efficient the current pathways are for detecting upper oesophageal cancer
standard: NHS England 62-day referral to treatment standard; NICE: urgent OGD for dysphagia and barium swallow not first line
finding: Of 348 oesophageal cancers, 14 cervical cases; 9 analysed. 6/9 first referred to ENT. 4/9 had OGD, 5/9 barium swallow (4/5 as first-line) and 7/9 rigid oesophagoscopy. Median GP referral to treatment 108 days vs 62-day standard.
setting: Head and neck and upper GI cancer pathways, Belfast City Hospital
cycle1_result: Of 348 oesophageal cancers, 14 cervical cases; 9 analysed. 6/9 first referred to ENT. 4/9 had OGD, 5/9 barium swallow (4/5 as first-line) and 7/9 rigid oesophagoscopy. Median GP referral to treatment 108 days vs 62-day standard.
other_findings: Authors recommend direct visualisation of the oesophagus for red flag dysphagia regardless of whether assessed by head and neck or upper GI pathway.

topic: Measurable oral liquid doses in children
title: AN AUDIT OF WHETHER PRESCRIBED DOSES ARE MEASURABLE ON THE GRADUATIONS OF ONE ORAL SYRINGE
standard: Local dispensing standard: prescribed volumes measurable on the printed graduations of one oral syringe
finding: Electronic prescriptions: 61/257 (24%) not measurable; paper charts: 57/303 (19%) not measurable (p=0.19). 77 of 457 liquid doses needed up to 4% adjustment and 10 up to 9%; 19/560 (3.4%) needed measuring to two decimal places.
change: Recommended dose rounding at prescribing and adding liquid strength information to local guidelines.
setting: Paediatric inpatient areas in one Trust (paper and electronic prescribing)
cycle1_result: Electronic prescriptions: 61/257 (24%) not measurable; paper charts: 57/303 (19%) not measurable (p=0.19). 77 of 457 liquid doses needed up to 4% adjustment and 10 up to 9%; 19/560 (3.4%) needed measuring to two decimal places.
intervention: Recommended dose rounding at prescribing and adding liquid strength information to local guidelines.
other_findings: Frequently non-measurable drugs included diazepam, alimemazine, chloral hydrate, azithromycin, metronidazole, paracetamol and ibuprofen; the electronic system had no automatic rounding.

title: AUDIT OF PARACETAMOL PRESCRIPTIONS IN PAEDIATRIC SURGICAL PATIENTS.

cycle1_result: Weight documented in 84% of inpatient and 94% of discharge prescriptions; height documented for no patient; IV/PO combined prescribing in 32 inpatients; of 52 on IV paracetamol, 20 not reviewed at 48 hours (only 3 appropriate).
intervention: Local guidelines amended in 2015 to dose obese children on lean body mass/ideal weight for height and reduce maximum daily dose to 75 mg/kg/day; education of prescribers recommended.
other_findings: 100 inpatient and 35 discharge prescriptions; overweight/obese children received doses up to 30 mg/kg (oral inpatient) and 33 mg/kg (discharge) based on ideal body weight.

title: CHILDREN'S WARFARIN CLINIC-AN AUDIT OF THE NEW PHARMACIST-LED TELEPHONE SERVICE BASED ON A UNIQUE COMPUTERISED SYSTEM COMPARED TO THE WARD BASED PAPER SYSTEM.
standard: NPSA safety standards for warfarin dosing
finding: Previous ward-based paper system: 44 patients, 1289 INRs; 11 patients (25%) lost to follow-up.

cycle1_result: Previous ward-based paper system: 44 patients, 1289 INRs; 11 patients (25%) lost to follow-up.
intervention: Pharmacist-led telephone warfarin service using a computerised documentation system replaced ward-based junior doctor dosing on paper.

title: AN AUDIT TO ASSESS THE TIMINGS OF TTAS AND INPATIENT ORDERS IN PAEDIATRICS; FROM WRITING, TO SCREENING, TO DISPENSING, AND TO LEAVING DISPENSARY.

standard: Local neonatal vancomycin guideline; 100% adherence
finding: Correct initial dose 28/28 (100%); level taken at correct time 13/15 (87%); 19/31 levels (62%) within 10–20 mg/L; all 6 levels >20 mg/L had next dose held, but follow-up adjustment often suboptimal; 3 of 4 low levels not acted on.
change: Guideline amended (single safe range 10–20 mg/L, doses adjusted on levels not age) and teaching sessions with worked examples planned for prescribers and nurses.
setting: Neonatal units
cycle1_result: Correct initial dose 28/28 (100%); level taken at correct time 13/15 (87%); 19/31 levels (62%) within 10–20 mg/L; all 6 levels >20 mg/L had next dose held, but follow-up adjustment often suboptimal; 3 of 4 low levels not acted on.
intervention: Guideline amended (single safe range 10–20 mg/L, doses adjusted on levels not age) and teaching sessions with worked examples planned for prescribers and nurses.

title: P26 An audit of the use of amikacin for early onset sepsis in premature neonates in an inpatient neonatal unit

finding: 100% adhered to guideline criteria and 100% prescribed 15 mg/kg; 12 (24%) had no level at 24 hours; of 38 with 24-hour levels only 6 (16%) were <5 mg/L; 17/23 (74%) in range at 36 hours; 2 patients received doses despite levels >5 mg/L.

intervention: Recommended change from 24-hourly to 36-hourly dosing; re-audit planned in one year.

authors: Caroline D; Tami B; Lidia T; Ioana G

other_findings: Evaluation using Datix-reported errors was planned 3 months after implementation, with monthly audit to follow.

topic: Influenza vaccination and asthma prescribing in children

standard: Local vancomycin prescribing and therapeutic drug monitoring guidance

cycle1_result: Loading, initial continuous dosing and TDM generally in line with local guidelines; 9% of first levels subtherapeutic; of 298 levels 56% therapeutic, 19% supratherapeutic, 25% subtherapeutic

title: P7 An audit of the management of resuscitation drugs and trolley contents
standard: Resuscitation Council (UK) acute care equipment and drug lists (2013) and local Trust trolley content list; daily trolley checks
finding: Drug content compliance 50%; oxygen cylinders on trolley 5/29; daily trolley checks 29/32; guidelines present on 31/32 trolleys but needed revision.

cycle1_result: Drug content compliance 50%; oxygen cylinders on trolley 5/29; daily trolley checks 29/32; guidelines present on 31/32 trolleys but needed revision.

cycle1_result: Only 16 patients (19%) met all eleven points; 27 (24.5%) fully compliant with blood monitoring frequency; TPMT measured in 104 (97%) but late in 48 (46%); weight and height not documented in 31 (28%) and 47 (43%); baseline VZV not checked in 23 (21%).

title: An audit on admission clerkings across Lancashire and South Cumbria NHS Foundation Trust (LSCFT)
standard: 20-item list of expected clerking components based on trust guidelines
finding: Highest completion: clerking within 6 hours, consultant face-to-face review within a week and current medication documentation. Lowest completion: clinical impression, bloods within 24 hours, capacity assessment and smoking/substance history (no percentages given).
change: Planned: standardised capacity assessment documentation and a clerking checklist; results presented at local teaching and recommendations sent to Site Tutors for local inductions.
setting: Chorley Mental Health Inpatient Unit, Lancashire and South Cumbria NHS Foundation Trust (psychiatric inpatient wards)
cycle1_result: Highest completion: clerking within 6 hours, consultant face-to-face review within a week and current medication documentation. Lowest completion: clinical impression, bloods within 24 hours, capacity assessment and smoking/substance history (no percentages given).
intervention: Planned: standardised capacity assessment documentation and a clerking checklist; results presented at local teaching and recommendations sent to Site Tutors for local inductions.
other_findings: Poorer clerkings were linked to poor patient engagement and transfer from another ward. A survey of 8 trainees found no uniform method for capacity documentation and no official clerking checklist.
authors: Edgell S; Sultan A; Hussain M
citation: Edgell S, Sultan A, Hussain M. An audit on admission clerkings across Lancashire and South Cumbria NHS Foundation Trust (LSCFT). BJPsych Open. 2021;7(S1):S319-S320. doi:10.1192/bjo.2021.842.

title: Audit of physical health monitoring during initiation and ongoing treatment with antipsychotic medication in a tier 3 outpatient CAMHS service, Belfast
standard: Belfast Trust CAMHS Antipsychotic Medication Monitoring Schedule (2015), based on CAMESA, NICE CG185, CG155 and Maudsley guidelines
finding: Baseline bloods (or declined) 92%; baseline ECG (or declined) 75%; complete monitoring bloods 33%; physical health parameters complete 42%; monitoring schedule present and current 42% (0% on PARIS)
change: Standardised recording of monitoring using PARIS clinic letters and the schedule at the front of clinical notes; baseline ECG made mandatory
setting: Child and Family Clinic, tier 3 outpatient CAMHS, Belfast Health and Social Care Trust
cycle1_result: Baseline bloods (or declined) 92%; baseline ECG (or declined) 75%; complete monitoring bloods 33%; physical health parameters complete 42%; monitoring schedule present and current 42% (0% on PARIS)
intervention: Standardised recording of monitoring using PARIS clinic letters and the schedule at the front of clinical notes; baseline ECG made mandatory
cycle2_result: Baseline bloods (or declined) 89%; baseline ECG (or declined) 67%; complete monitoring bloods 44%; parameters complete 56%; schedule present and current 38%, present but not current 50% (0% on PARIS)

authors: Hamlyn P; McMenamin A; Boyd H; Patton L

title: Clinical audit on possible causes of hospital initiated clinic cancellations and recommendation to improve the service
standard: Trust protocol: clinics cancelled only when absolutely necessary and patients informed at least 8 weeks before the appointed clinic
finding: About 54% of 193 booked clinics were cancelled (68% in September, 30.30% in August). Around 50% of patients were informed 8 weeks in advance. Causes: junior doctor on call 31.58%, annual leave 25%, study leave 21%.
setting: Inner city community mental health team (CMHT) outpatient clinics
cycle1_result: About 54% of 193 booked clinics were cancelled (68% in September, 30.30% in August). Around 50% of patients were informed 8 weeks in advance. Causes: junior doctor on call 31.58%, annual leave 25%, study leave 21%.
other_findings: 72% of cancellations were by junior doctors and 28% by consultants; poor communication between clinicians and the appointment booking team was the main cause.
authors: Haque T; Ibrahim M; Ravindranath B
citation: Haque T, Ibrahim M, Ravindranath B. Clinical audit on possible causes of hospital initiated clinic cancellations and recommendation to improve the service. BJPsych Open. 2021;7(S1):S324-S324. doi:10.1192/bjo.2021.853.

title: An audit into the physical health monitoring of patients who are prescribed antipsychotics in HMP Birmingham

finding: Pre-prescription, 12-weekly and annual physical health checks had poor compliance; checks that were done coincided with diabetic reviews

cycle1_result: Pre-prescription, 12-weekly and annual physical health checks had poor compliance; checks that were done coincided with diabetic reviews

title: Has vitamin D had its day? An audit of vitamin D, prolactin and HBA1C monitoring over one year in an in-patient secure service
standard: Best practice: at least annual HbA1c and prolactin for all; vitamin D only if symptomatic of deficiency
finding: 100% tested on the medium secure unit, but vitamin D tested without documented clinical indication; on the other units prolactin and HbA1c were least measured (18% male LSU, 23% female ward); vitamin D testing 38% female ward and 18% male ward.
change: Recommended adding prolactin and HbA1c to pre-CPA physical screens and stopping vitamin D testing without symptoms.
setting: Five in-patient secure wards (medium and low secure, including Northside House)
cycle1_result: 100% tested on the medium secure unit, but vitamin D tested without documented clinical indication; on the other units prolactin and HbA1c were least measured (18% male LSU, 23% female ward); vitamin D testing 38% female ward and 18% male ward.
intervention: Recommended adding prolactin and HbA1c to pre-CPA physical screens and stopping vitamin D testing without symptoms.
other_findings: The unit with a dedicated physical health team scored 100%; prolactin levels were highest on male medium secure wards.
authors: Lujanschi O; Thomas T
citation: Lujanschi O, Thomas T. Has vitamin D had its day? An audit of vitamin D, prolactin and HBA1C monitoring over one year in an in-patient secure service. BJPsych Open. 2021;7(S1):S330-S331. doi:10.1192/bjo.2021.868.

topic: Physical health assessment on psychiatric admission
title: Improving Admission Clerking and Physical Health Checks in Acute Psychiatric Inpatients. A Quality Improvement Project (QIP)
standard: Local and NHS trust admission protocol: clerking, mental state examination, physical examination, ECG and routine bloods all completed within 72 hours of admission
finding: All five criteria completed within 72 hours in 27 patients (62.8%); delayed in 14 (33.6%); 2 (4.7%) refused blood tests.

setting: Battersea Bridge House Hospital, 22-bed acute mental health facility (three wards)
cycle1_result: All five criteria completed within 72 hours in 27 patients (62.8%); delayed in 14 (33.6%); 2 (4.7%) refused blood tests.

cycle2_result: Overall compliance for physical health checks increased from 62.4% to 96.6% after intervention; reported 1.76-fold increase in timely protocol completion, 1.39-fold reduction in delays and 4-fold drop in patient refusal.

title: Review DebrIeF: a collaborative distributed leadership approach to "hot debrief" after cardiac arrest in the emergency department - a quality improvement project.
standard: Hot debrief after cardiac arrest (American Heart Association recommendation; Royal College QI requirements)
finding: Audit identified zero hot debriefs occurring in 2019 (0%).

setting: Emergency Department, Doncaster Royal Infirmary, Doncaster and Bassetlaw Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust

intervention: Four PDSA cycles (March 2020 to September 2021) using staff surveys and interviews to co-design and implement an ED hot debrief tool with a nurse-led distributed leadership approach.
